newsitem.title: USA: Perot asks court to add him to U.S. debates.
newsitem.headline: Perot asks court to add him to U.S. debates.

text.p: Reform Party presidential nominee Ross Perot filed suit on Monday seeking federal government backing for his bid to force his way into campaign debates between President Bill Clinton and Republican nominee Bob Dole.

Lawyers for Perot and his running mate, economist Pat Choate, filed papers in U.S. District Court in Washington essentially asking an injunction against debates already scheduled that would exclude Perot, and demanding that he and Choate be included in any debates that are held.
It was not clear when the court would proceed with the lawsuit although speculation centred on Thursday as a possible date for the hearing of arguments.

The Dole and Clinton camps agreed over the weekend to hold two one-on-one televised presidential debates between their candidates on October 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, and October 16 in San Diego, California.

In so doing, Clinton gave up his support of Perot's demand to be included and yielded to Dole, who opposed participation by the feisty Texas billionaire, and to the recommendation of a private bipartisan debates commission that the clash be limited to the two major party candidates.
The two campaigns also agreed to hold a vice presidential debate on October 9 in St. Petersburg, Florida, but limit it to Vice President Al Gore and Republican Jack Kemp.

The Perot camp cried foul, portraying the move as an establishment effort to smother a third-party candidate who won 19 percent of the popular vote in the 1992 presidential election after making a strong mark in that year's debates.

"We are here this morning because there is no more fundamental exercise of free speech in this country than the right to vote for the candidate of your choice," Perot campaign spokesman Russell Verney told reporters at the court.
He said a Louis Harris poll found that 76 percent of voters want Perot included in the debates as he was in 1992.

Perot's suit named the Federal Election Commission, which oversees campaign financing laws but has not been involved in debate preparations, as the agency that shoud be directed to have the Reform Party candidates included. It argues that the debate commission, a privately funded agency established by the two major parties to organise the debates in the 1980s, is a fraudulent entity.

"The Republicans and Democrats have joined to get them (the FEC) to put up a fraudulent front organisation, the Commission on Presidential Debates, to control the debates and keep third-party candidates out of the debates," Verney said.

The commission recommended last week that Perot should not be invited because it felt he had no realistic chance of winning. Current opinion polls show him garnering only five or six percent backing, with Clinton solidly in the lead and Dole his only close competition.

The move to exclude Perot was pressed by the Dole camp, which sees the feisty Texan as more a threat to their candidate than to Clinton. The Clinton camp yielded in return for Dole concessions on other debate terms.
Perot has since treated Dole and the commission to the withering sarcastic tongue-lashings that are his hallmark.

"Now here is a guy who is supposed to be a war hero," he said of Dole, a decorated and combat-wounded veteran of World War II, in an NBC interview on Sunday. "You'd think he'd be willing to talk to another person, wouldn't you?"

Perot argues that the debate commission -- which did invite him into the 1992 presidential campaign debates, where he aimed most of his fire at Clinton's rival, then-President George Bush -- simply does the bidding of the two major parties, which founded it.

"They (the established parties) do not want to discuss the issues that will determine this country's future," Perot said in the NBC interview. "They don't want to talk about the debt, the deficit, they don't want to talk about setting the highest ethical standards for the White House and the Congress."
